overview: Kushan Principalities is this atlas’s uncertain label for a broad northwestern region around 500-600, including Gandhara, Swat and neighbouring valleys. It should not imply that the earlier Kushan Empire survived intact. Kidarite remnants are documented chiefly before 500; distinct later rulers governed this region. The outline is not a securely reconstructed common frontier.

periods.title: Earlier successor kingdoms
periods.summary: Kidarite rulers adopted Kushan royal traditions; their regional chronology remains debated.

periods.title: The imported map interval
periods.summary: Trade, Buddhist patronage and regional artistic exchange continued amid political fragmentation.

periods.title: Later religious continuity
periods.summary: Takht-i-Bahi remained in use into the seventh century.

items.text: The Kidarites controlled Tokharistan and later Gandhara, but they lost their northern kingdom in 467. A surviving Gandharan kingdom, perhaps in Swat, sent embassies to China until 477. These are important predecessors to the map interval, rather than evidence for an unchanged Kushan government in 600.

A royal title could outlive its original dynasty. Kidarite rulers used Kushanshah, or king of the Kushans, and some earlier coin designs continued under new rulers. Coins therefore need their own careful chronology: a familiar name on money does not automatically identify the government that issued it.

The Schøyen copper scroll records a Buddhist foundation involving Alchon rulers, including Khingila, Toramana, Mehama and Javukha. Its date is usually placed in the 490s, with different proposed calendar conversions. These rulers belong to the region’s Hunnic political history and must not simply be renamed Kushan princes.

Mountain passes carried more than armies. Routes through the Khyber and Karakoram connected Gandhara and Swat with wider trading networks. Donations supported Buddhist images, and sixth-century art linked communities across present-day Pakistan, Afghanistan, India and Central Asia.

Around 520, the Chinese traveller Song Yun’s account describes the ruler of Udyana, in the Swat region, eating vegetarian food and turning to government business after midday worship. This is a portrait of one royal routine, not a menu for every local family.

The same account describes grain and fruit harvests, night-time bells, and flowers gathered by monks and laypeople as offerings. Court worship included drums, conches, lutes, harps and pipes. A religious gathering could be a very noisy occasion!

At Takht-i-Bahi, the surviving monastery contains meditation cells, meeting space, courtyards for stupas and covered stairways. The complex developed over centuries and remained occupied into the seventh century. Its plan lets us follow routes between quieter rooms and shared gathering places.

Builders used dressed and partly dressed local stone with lime and mud mortar. Takht-i-Bahi spreads across hilltops, so stairs and changes in level are part of the experience. Reaching a meeting there required more climbing than walking into a modern classroom.

sections.title: Families, learning and a written voice

items.text: The copper scroll’s donor group includes parents, a wife and women associated with major monasteries, Arccavamana and Sasa. Elite religious giving could involve a family network with women named in their own right.

A short Sanskrit phrase in the scroll is सार्धं पित्रा ओपन्देन, sārdhaṃ pitrā Opandena: “together with his father Opanda.” The display uses modern Devanagari to transcribe the original Brahmi-family lettering. This is an Alchon-period regional witness from around 500, not a securely identified record of a sixth-century Kushan state.

The scroll also names the religious teacher Ratnagama and copies Buddhist scripture and a philosophical verse associated with Nagarjuna. Commissioning it required people able to compose, copy and engrave Sanskrit, although it tells us little about ordinary children’s schooling.

One blessing asks for freedom from famine, illness and disputes. These were urgent hopes expressed through religious giving. The prayer supplies evidence of concern for health and food security, without documenting a hospital, treatment or sanitation system.

Where was this foundation? Scholars disagree. Hans Bakker argues for a Punjab and Kashmir setting instead of the earlier Bactrian interpretation, and suggests that a royal woman helped organize it. The scroll is valuable, but its uncertain provenance cannot pin a capital onto this map.

A tiny earlier clue travelled into a shrine: a Kidarite silver coin, only 27 millimetres across, came from a relic deposit at Hadda Stupa 10. Charles Masson excavated the deposit in 1834; his drawing later helped the British Museum identify the coin’s original context.

A Gandharan brass Buddha dated to about the late sixth century stands just 33.7 centimetres tall. Its style combines local sculptural traditions with Gupta influences from northern India. Small portable images helped artistic ideas travel with people: this Buddha did not need a moving van.

Archaeologists found late Sasanian and Hunnic coins at Buddhist sites, including coins in relic deposits at Dharmarajika and Manikyala. Such deposits show that particular shrines still received gifts after the region’s political changes. A monastery’s story can outlast the dynasty in the textbook.

The evidence also includes fewer coins after 500 and declining building patronage. Yet some monasteries remained occupied and even received limited new construction. Broken sculptures and deserted buildings therefore need careful interpretation; they do not establish one simultaneous destruction of every Buddhist community.

ending.text: The atlas stops this label in 600, but no securely identified united “Kushan Principalities” state can be assigned a single fall in that year. The region underwent several political transitions, while Buddhist institutions and artistic traditions continued unevenly. Decline and survival happened at different sites and times.
